claim: The mammalian Mitochondrial Pyruvate Carrier (MPC) comprises two obligate, paralogous subunits, MPC1 and MPC2.
source: The mammalian Mitochondrial Pyruvate Carrier (MPC) comprises two obligate, paralogous subunits, MPC1 and MPC2.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the MPC structure.

claim: Loss of either MPC subunit results in destabilization and loss of the other subunit and thus the MPC complex.
source: Loss of either subunit results in destabilization and loss of the other subunit and thus the MPC complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MPC subunit interdependence.

claim: Skeletal muscle-specific MPC knockout mice (MPC SkmKO) were generated by crossing mice with a floxed Mpc1 allele with mice expressing Cre under control of a Myogenin promoter.
source: We generated skeletal muscle-specific MPC knockout mice (MPC SkmKO) by crossing mice with a floxed Mpc1 allele (Mpc1fl) (Gray et al., 2015) with mice expressing Cre under control of a Myogenin promoter (Myogenin-Cre) (Figure 1A) (Fink et al., 2018; Li et al., 2005).
evidence: The generation method is described in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Myogenin-Cre selectively recombines floxed alleles in skeletal muscle.
source: Myogenin-Cre selectively recombines floxed alleles in skeletal muscle.
evidence: This is cited knowledge about the Myogenin-Cre system.

claim: Western blots confirmed selective loss of MPC1 and MPC2 proteins in MPC SkmKO mouse muscles.
source: Western blots confirmed selective loss of MPC1and MPC2 proteins in MPC SkmKO mouse muscles (Figure 1B).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 1B demonstrates protein loss.

claim: Mpc1 but not Mpc2 mRNA was lost in MPC SkmKO mice.
source: Mpc1 but not Mpc2 mRNA was also lost (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: mRNA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: MPC disruption abolished 14C-labeled pyruvate uptake in isolated skeletal muscle mitochondria.
source: In assays with isolated skeletal muscle mitochondria, MPC disruption abolished 14C-labeled pyruvate uptake and markedly decreased pyruvate-driven respiration (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Pyruvate uptake assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: MPC disruption markedly decreased pyruvate-driven respiration in isolated skeletal muscle mitochondria.
source: In assays with isolated skeletal muscle mitochondria, MPC disruption abolished 14C-labeled pyruvate uptake and markedly decreased pyruvate-driven respiration (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Respiration data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Glutamate oxidation was not different between WT and MPC SkmKO mice.
source: In contrast, glutamate oxidation and markers of electron transport chain complexes were not different (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Glutamate oxidation data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Markers of electron transport chain complexes were not different between WT and MPC SkmKO mice.
source: In contrast, glutamate oxidation and markers of electron transport chain complexes were not different (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Western blot data for ETC complexes shown in Figure 1F.

claim: MPC disruption causes a selective defect in mitochondrial pyruvate metabolism.
source: These results are consistent with MPC disruption causing a selective defect in mitochondrial pyruvate metabolism.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing abolished pyruvate uptake and respiration but normal glutamate oxidation and ETC markers.

claim: WT and MPC SkmKO mouse grip strength was not different.
source: WT and MPC SkmKO mouse grip strength was not different nor was ex vivo muscle force production (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Grip strength data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Ex vivo muscle force production was not different between WT and MPC SkmKO mice.
source: WT and MPC SkmKO mouse grip strength was not different nor was ex vivo muscle force production (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Ex vivo force production data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: MPC SkmKO mice fatigued earlier during treadmill running exercise tolerance tests.
source: In contrast, MPC SkmKO mice fatigued earlier during treadmill running exercise tolerance tests (Figure 2B).
evidence: Exercise tolerance test data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: MPC SkmKO mice exhibited similar food intake to WT mice in home cage living.
source: In home cage living, MPC SkmKO mice exhibited similar food intake, mildly elevated VO2, decreased RER, and unchanged voluntary locomotion (Figure 2C, D, E and F).
evidence: Food intake data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MPC SkmKO mice exhibited mildly elevated VO2 in home cage living.
source: In home cage living, MPC SkmKO mice exhibited similar food intake, mildly elevated VO2, decreased RER, and unchanged voluntary locomotion (Figure 2C, D, E and F).
evidence: VO2 data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: MPC SkmKO mice exhibited decreased RER in home cage living.
source: In home cage living, MPC SkmKO mice exhibited similar food intake, mildly elevated VO2, decreased RER, and unchanged voluntary locomotion (Figure 2C, D, E and F).
evidence: RER data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: MPC SkmKO mice exhibited unchanged voluntary locomotion in home cage living.
source: In home cage living, MPC SkmKO mice exhibited similar food intake, mildly elevated VO2, decreased RER, and unchanged voluntary locomotion (Figure 2C, D, E and F).
evidence: Locomotion data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Muscle glycogen content was unchanged between WT and MPC SkmKO mice.
source: Muscle glycogen content as a measure of muscle energy balance was also unchanged (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Glycogen content data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Basal MPC SkmKO muscle function is maintained by adaptive mechanisms that increase metabolic rate but cannot support the greater energetic demands of exercise.
source: These results indicate that basal MPC SkmKO muscle function is maintained by adaptive mechanisms that increase metabolic rate but cannot support the greater energetic demands of exercise.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of normal grip strength, normal glycogen, increased VO2, but decreased exercise tolerance.

claim: WT and MPC SkmKO mice are initially indistinguishable by body weight and composition.
source: By body weight and composition, WT and MPC SkmKO mice are initially indistinguishable.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by body composition data in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Beginning about 13 weeks of age, MPC SkmKO mice display a striking resistance to fat mass gains, with perfect lean mass sparing.
source: Surprisingly, beginning about 13 weeks of age, MPC SkmKO mice display a striking resistance to fat mass gains, with perfect lean mass sparing (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Body composition data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: MPC SkmKO mouse leanness and normal grip strength persists through 40 weeks of age.
source: MPC SkmKO mouse leanness and normal grip strength persists through 40 weeks of age (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Long-term body composition and grip strength data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Serum FGF21 was not increased in MPC SkmKO mice.
source: Interestingly, serum FGF21 was not increased in MPC SkmKO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: FGF21 measurement data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In other mouse models of muscle mitochondrial stress, dramatically increased FGF21 leads to decreased adiposity.
source: This is notable because it contrasts with other mouse models of muscle mitochondrial stress, where dramatically increased FGF21 leads to decreased adiposity (Pereira et al., 2017; Tezze et al., 2017; Voigt et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from other studies.

claim: Female WT and MPC SkmKO mice showed similar MPC SkmKO mouse leanness at 28 weeks.
source: Although male mice were used throughout this study, we followed a cohort of female WT and MPC SkmKO mice for 28 weeks and observed similar MPC SkmKO mouse leanness (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Female mouse body composition data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Myogenin Cre expression in Mpc1+/+ mice did not affect body composition.
source: In an important control experiment, Myogenin Cre expression in Mpc1+/+ mice did not affect body composition, indicating Mpc1 deletion but not the presence of Cre causes MPC SkmKO leanness (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Control experiment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mpc1 deletion but not the presence of Cre causes MPC SkmKO leanness.
source: In an important control experiment, Myogenin Cre expression in Mpc1+/+ mice did not affect body composition, indicating Mpc1 deletion but not the presence of Cre causes MPC SkmKO leanness (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the control experiment data.

claim: Relative 3H partitioning into the aqueous versus organic fraction was greater in MPC SkmKO muscle, indicating increased fatty acid uptake and oxidation.
source: Relative 3H partitioning into the aqueous versus organic fraction, which increases with fatty chain shortening, was greater in MPC SkmKO muscle, indicating increased fatty acid uptake and oxidation (Figure 3C).
evidence: Triolein uptake assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MPC SkmKO muscle manifested greater complete and partial palmitate oxidation ex vivo.
source: MPC SkmKO muscle manifested greater complete and partial palmitate oxidation (Figure 3D).
evidence: Ex vivo palmitate oxidation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: At age 7 weeks, before onset of MPC SkmKO mouse leanness, glucose tolerance tests revealed a minimal decrease in MPC SkmKO mouse glucose tolerance, with slightly increased lactate excursion.
source: Glucose tolerance tests (GTTs) at age 7 weeks, before onset of MPC SkmKO mouse leanness, revealed a minimal decrease in MPC SkmKO mouse glucose tolerance, with slightly increased lactate excursion (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: GTT data for young mice shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: At age 36 weeks, well after onset of MPC SkmKO mouse leanness, glucose tolerance was mildly improved and lactate excursion was markedly increased.
source: In contrast, at age 36 weeks, well after onset of MPC SkmKO mouse leanness, glucose tolerance was mildly improved and lactate excursion was markedly increased (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: GTT data for old mice shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: Glucose infusion rate (GIR) was moderately greater in MPC SkmKO mice during steady state of hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamps, indicating greater whole-body insulin sensitivity.
source: Glucose infusion rate (GIR) was moderately greater in MPC SkmKO mice during steady state, indicating greater whole-body insulin sensitivity (Figure 4B).
evidence: GIR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Under basal conditions, MPC SkmKO mice showed increased hepatic glucose production (Ra) and peripheral disposal (Rd), indicating elevated glucose turnover, or Cori Cycling.
source: Under basal conditions, MPC SkmKO mice showed increased hepatic glucose production (Ra) and peripheral disposal (Rd), indicating elevated glucose turnover, or Cori Cycling (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Ra and Rd data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Under clamped steady state conditions, MPC SkmKO mice showed no difference in Ra but significantly greater Rd.
source: In contrast, under clamped steady state conditions, when insulin is increased by exogenous administration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), MPC SkmKO mice showed no difference in Ra but significantly greater Rd (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Ra and Rd data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Clamped steady state MPC SkmKO muscle glucose uptake was strikingly increased.
source: Notably, clamped steady state MPC SkmKO muscle glucose uptake and blood lactate levels were strikingly increased (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: Muscle glucose uptake data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Clamped steady state blood lactate levels were strikingly increased in MPC SkmKO mice.
source: Notably, clamped steady state MPC SkmKO muscle glucose uptake and blood lactate levels were strikingly increased (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: Blood lactate data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Western blots of mixed quadriceps muscle harvested at the end of clamps did not show increased MPC SkmKO muscle Akt serine 473, AMPK threonine 172 phosphorylation, or PDH E1α serine 232 phosphorylation.
source: Western blots of mixed quadriceps muscle harvested at the end of clamps did not show increased MPC SkmKO muscle Akt serine 473, AMPK threonine 172 phosphorylation, or PDH E1α serine 232 phosphorylation, indicating that if these regulatory protein modifications contributed to increased MPC SkmKO glucose uptake that they did not persist until time of analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Under basal conditions, constitutively elevated muscle lactate excretion in MPC SkmKO mice drives increased hepatic gluconeogenesis and Cori Cycling.
source: Under basal conditions, constitutively elevated muscle lactate excretion in MPC SkmKO mice drives increased hepatic gluconeogenesis and Cori Cycling.
evidence: This is inferred from the clamp data showing increased Ra and Rd under basal conditions.

claim: Under clamped steady state conditions, insulin administration supersedes mass action and suppresses gluconeogenesis proportionately greater in MPC SkmKO mice to equal that of WT mice.
source: Under clamped steady state conditions, insulin administration supersedes mass action and suppresses gluconeogenesis proportionately greater in MPC SkmKO mice to equal that of WT mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the clamp data showing no difference in Ra under clamped conditions despite increased basal Ra.

claim: Muscle MPC disruption moderately increased metabolic flexibility of the liver.
source: Thus, muscle MPC disruption moderately increased metabolic flexibility of the liver.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential hepatic glucose production responses under basal vs. clamped conditions.

claim: Compared to WT muscle, MPC SkmKO muscle fatigued more rapidly when stimulated with one twitch per second (1 Hz).
source: Compared to WT muscle, MPC SkmKO muscle fatigued more rapidly when stimulated with one twitch per second (1 Hz) but similarly when stimulated with one twitch per two seconds (0.5 Hz) (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Muscle contraction data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: WT and MPC SkmKO muscle fatigued similarly when stimulated with one twitch per two seconds (0.5 Hz).
source: Compared to WT muscle, MPC SkmKO muscle fatigued more rapidly when stimulated with one twitch per second (1 Hz) but similarly when stimulated with one twitch per two seconds (0.5 Hz) (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Muscle contraction data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Principal component analysis demonstrated distinct effects of both contraction and genotype on muscle metabolites.
source: Principal component analysis demonstrated distinct effects of both contraction and genotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: PCA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Compared to contracted WT muscle, contracted MPC SkmKO muscle pyruvate levels were several fold greater.
source: Compared to contracted WT muscle, contracted MPC SkmKO muscle pyruvate levels were several fold greater; conversely, lactate was similarly increased in contracted WT and SkmKO muscle (Figure 5B).
evidence: Metabolite data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Lactate was similarly increased in contracted WT and SkmKO muscle.
source: Compared to contracted WT muscle, contracted MPC SkmKO muscle pyruvate levels were several fold greater; conversely, lactate was similarly increased in contracted WT and SkmKO muscle (Figure 5B).
evidence: Metabolite data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Contraction increases glycolytic production of pyruvate that is readily oxidized by WT but not SkmKO muscle.
source: These results suggest contraction increases glycolytic production of pyruvate that is readily oxidized by WT but not SkmKO muscle.
evidence: This is inferred from the pyruvate and lactate data during contraction.

claim: The lactate:pyruvate ratio was markedly greater in contracted WT compared to MPC SkmKO muscle.
source: Pyruvate and lactate rapidly equilibrate across lactate dehydrogenase utilizing NADH and NAD+ as co-factors. Accordingly, the lactate:pyruvate ratio, which was markedly greater in contracted WT compared to MPC SkmKO muscle, is often reflected by the NADH:NAD+ ratio.
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolite data in Figure 5B.

claim: NAD+ was unchanged between WT and MPC SkmKO muscle during contraction.
source: This is precisely what we observed here, where NAD+ was unchanged and NADH was decreased in MPC SkmKO muscle during contraction (Figure 5B).
evidence: Metabolite data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: NADH was decreased in MPC SkmKO muscle during contraction.
source: This is precisely what we observed here, where NAD+ was unchanged and NADH was decreased in MPC SkmKO muscle during contraction (Figure 5B).
evidence: Metabolite data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In muscle the NADH pool is several fold greater than the NAD+ pool.
source: Of note, in muscle the NADH pool is several fold greater than the NAD+ pool (Steen and Vesth, 1979).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from a previous study.

claim: MPC disruption decreased isocitrate/citrate and malate in muscle.
source: MPC disruption decreased isocitrate/citrate and malate, and abolished contraction-induced increases in succinate (Figure 5C).
evidence: Metabolite data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: MPC disruption abolished contraction-induced increases in succinate.
source: MPC disruption decreased isocitrate/citrate and malate, and abolished contraction-induced increases in succinate (Figure 5C).
evidence: Metabolite data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No genotype effect was observed for α-ketoglutarate.
source: In contrast, no genotype effect was observed for α-ketoglutarate (αKG), which may be derived from glutamate independently of pyruvate fluxes (Figure 5C).
evidence: Metabolite data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: α-ketoglutarate may be derived from glutamate independently of pyruvate fluxes.
source: In contrast, no genotype effect was observed for α-ketoglutarate (αKG), which may be derived from glutamate independently of pyruvate fluxes (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for the αKG data.

claim: The decreased lactate:pyruvate ratio, NADH:NAD+ ratio, and TCA cycle metabolite levels in SkmKO muscle demonstrate a shift to a more oxidized state.
source: Together, the decreased lactate:pyruvate ratio, NADH:NAD+ ratio, and TCA cycle metabolite levels in SkmKO muscle convincingly demonstrate a shift to a more oxidized state.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined metabolite data.

claim: The shift to a more oxidized state in SkmKO muscle is consistent with impaired capacity to generate reducing equivalents from pyruvate, resulting in transfer of reductive drive to the liver in the form of lactate.
source: This is consistent with impaired capacity to generate reducing equivalents from pyruvate, resulting in transfer of reductive drive to the liver in the form of lactate.
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolite data and the concept of Cori cycling.

claim: Muscle acyl-carnitine accumulation and mitochondrial overload is associated with insulin resistance in T2D.
source: Muscle acyl-carnitine accumulation and mitochondrial overload is associated with insulin resistance in T2D (Koves et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from a previous study.

claim: MPC disruption strikingly attenuated contraction-induced increases in acyl-carnitine content.
source: Indeed, MPC disruption strikingly attenuated contraction-induced increases in acyl-carnitine content (Figure 5D).
evidence: Acyl-carnitine data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: No main effects of genotype were observed for carnitine levels.
source: No main effects of genotype were observed for carnitine levels, indicating free carnitine was not a limiting substrate for acyl-carnitine production (Figure 5D).
evidence: Carnitine data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Free carnitine was not a limiting substrate for acyl-carnitine production.
source: No main effects of genotype were observed for carnitine levels, indicating free carnitine was not a limiting substrate for acyl-carnitine production (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is inferred from the carnitine data.

claim: Increased fatty acid oxidation in MPC SkmKO muscle suggests lower acyl-carnitine levels result from increased oxidation rather than decreased production.
source: Lower acyl-carnitine levels in contracted MPC SkmKO muscle could result from either decreased production or increased oxidation. Our observations of increased fatty acid oxidation in MPC SkmKO muscle suggest the latter.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of lower acyl-carnitine levels and increased fatty acid oxidation.

claim: qPCR measurements showed no differences between WT and MPC SkmKO mice for the key fatty acid oxidation enzyme transcripts Cpt1b, Echs1, and Hadha.
source: qPCR measurements showed no differences between WT and MPC SkmKO mice for the key fatty acid oxidation enzyme transcripts Cpt1b, Echs1, and Hadha (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Programmatic upregulation of fatty acid oxidation gene expression does not underlie increased MPC SkmKO muscle fatty acid oxidation.
source: These results indicate programmatic upregulation of fatty acid oxidation gene expression does not underlie increased MPC SkmKO muscle fatty acid oxidation.
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR data showing no changes in fatty acid oxidation enzyme transcripts.

claim: Contracted MPC SkmKO muscle citrate levels were decreased.
source: In addition to our observation that contracted MPC SkmKO muscle citrate levels were decreased, we observed decreased flux of intraperitoneally-injected (U)13C-glucose into muscle citrate, simultaneous with increased flux of 13C into the liver citrate (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Citrate data shown in Figure 5C and 13C-glucose tracing data in Figure 5E.

claim: Decreased flux of intraperitoneally-injected (U)13C-glucose into muscle citrate was observed in MPC SkmKO mice.
source: In addition to our observation that contracted MPC SkmKO muscle citrate levels were decreased, we observed decreased flux of intraperitoneally-injected (U)13C-glucose into muscle citrate, simultaneous with increased flux of 13C into the liver citrate (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: 13C-glucose tracing data shown in Figure 5E and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Increased flux of 13C into the liver citrate was observed in MPC SkmKO mice.
source: In addition to our observation that contracted MPC SkmKO muscle citrate levels were decreased, we observed decreased flux of intraperitoneally-injected (U)13C-glucose into muscle citrate, simultaneous with increased flux of 13C into the liver citrate (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: 13C-glucose tracing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The combination of decreased and increased glucose enrichments into muscle and liver TCA cycle intermediates, respectively, is consistent with the elevated Cori Cycling observed during glucose clamps.
source: The combination of decreased and increased glucose enrichments into muscle and liver TCA cycle intermediates, respectively, is consistent with the elevated Cori Cycling we observed during glucose clamps.
evidence: This is inferred from the 13C-glucose tracing data and the clamp data.

claim: MPC SkmKO muscle malonyl-CoA levels were decreased.
source: In a separate experiment under similar conditions but without glucose injection, MPC SkmKO muscle malonyl-CoA levels were decreased (Figure 5F).
evidence: Malonyl-CoA data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Decreased muscle pyruvate flux through citrate could propagate to decreased malonyl-CoA production and a regulated fatty acid oxidation increase by Cpt1b disinhibition.
source: Decreased muscle pyruvate flux through citrate could also propagate to decreased malonyl-CoA production and a regulated fatty acid oxidation increase by Cpt1b disinhibition.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on known metabolic pathways.

claim: The minimal MPC SkmKO muscle increase in acetyl-carnitine is consistent with diminished substrate competition from mitochondrial pyruvate for entry into the mitochondrial acetyl-CoA pool.
source: In accord, the minimal MPC SkmKO muscle increase in acetyl-carnitine, which is chemically adjacent to acetyl-CoA, is consistent with diminished substrate competition from mitochondrial pyruvate for entry into the mitochondrial acetyl-CoA pool.
evidence: This is inferred from the acetyl-carnitine data and metabolic pathway knowledge.

claim: Decreased TCA cycle pyruvate entry in MPC SkmKO muscle leads to increased fatty acid oxidation by both disinhibition of Cpt1b and diminished substrate competition, with the latter predominating in working muscle.
source: These observations suggest decreased TCA cycle pyruvate entry in MPC SkmKO muscle leads to increased fatty acid oxidation by both disinhibition of Cpt1b and diminished substrate competition, with the latter predominating in working muscle.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on malonyl-CoA, acyl-carnitines, and fatty acid oxidation.

claim: Increased fatty acid oxidation can only partially compensate for decreased pyruvate oxidation, because it requires but does not generate oxaloacetate.
source: Increased fatty acid oxidation can only partially compensate for decreased pyruvate oxidation, because it requires but does not generate oxaloacetate.
evidence: This is based on metabolic pathway knowledge.

claim: In contrast to the accumulation of pyruvate in MPC SkmKO muscle with contraction, glutamine and glutamate were depleted.
source: In contrast to the accumulation of pyruvate we observed in MPC SkmKO muscle with contraction, glutamine and glutamate were depleted (Figure 5G).
evidence: Amino acid data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: MPC disruption increases glutaminolysis in skeletal muscle.
source: Glutamine is a major cellular fuel, and our results suggest that MPC disruption increases glutaminolysis in skeletal muscle as previously observed in cancer cell and liver systems (Gray et al., 2015; Vacanti et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the glutamine/glutamate depletion data and cited knowledge from other systems.

claim: Alanine was increased similarly by contraction in both WT and MPC SkmKO muscle.
source: Alanine was increased similarly by contraction in both WT and MPC SkmKO muscle whereas aspartate was markedly increased in SkmKO muscle only (Figure 5H).
evidence: Amino acid data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Aspartate was markedly increased in SkmKO muscle only during contraction.
source: Alanine was increased similarly by contraction in both WT and MPC SkmKO muscle whereas aspartate was markedly increased in SkmKO muscle only (Figure 5H).
evidence: Amino acid data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Pyruvate-alanine cycling can enable MPC-independent pyruvate carboxylation, which could increase aspartate by mitochondrial transamination of oxaloacetate.
source: Pyruvate-alanine cycling can enable MPC-independent pyruvate carboxylation, which could increase aspartate by mitochondrial transamination of oxaloacetate.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on metabolic pathway knowledge.

claim: Pyruvate-alanine cycling enables MPC-independent mitochondrial pyruvate utilization in fibroblasts and liver.
source: We and others previously found that pyruvate-alanine cycling enables MPC-independent mitochondrial pyruvate utilization in fibroblasts and liver (Bowman et al., 2016; Gray et al., 2015; McCommis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from previous studies.

claim: In pyruvate-alanine cycling, pyruvate is transaminated in the cytosol to alanine, imported into the mitochondrial matrix by a currently unknown alanine transporter, and then deaminated back to pyruvate for oxidation.
source: In this case, pyruvate is transaminated in the cytosol to alanine, imported into the mitochondrial matrix by a currently unknown alanine transporter, and then deaminated back to pyruvate for oxidation.
evidence: This is a description of the pyruvate-alanine cycling mechanism based on knowledge.

claim: (U)13C-glucose flux into alanine was increased in MPC SkmKO muscle, consistent with pyruvate-alanine cycling.
source: Here, in addition to our observation that (U)13C-glucose flux into citrate was decreased in MPC SkmKO muscle, we observed that (U)13C-glucose flux into alanine was increased in MPC SkmKO muscle, consistent with pyruvate-alanine cycling (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: 13C-glucose tracing data shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Succinate restored respiration to pre-inhibited levels after MPC and alanine transaminase inhibition, indicating maintenance of gross mitochondrial oxidative capacity.
source: Succinate restored respiration to pre-inhibited levels, indicating maintenance of gross mitochondrial oxidative capacity.
evidence: This is stated based on the respiration rescue experiment data in Figure 5I.

claim: The additive effect of MPC and alanine transaminase inhibition on pyruvate-driven respiration provides evidence for pyruvate-alanine cycling as a mechanism for MPC-independent carbohydrate oxidation in MPC SkmKO muscle.
source: These results provide evidence for pyruvate-alanine cycling as a mechanism for MPC-independent carbohydrate oxidation in MPC SkmKO muscle.
evidence: This is inferred from the additive inhibition experiment data.

claim: Pyruvate-alanine cycling is kinetically limited compared to direct mitochondrial pyruvate uptake.
source: Combined with our observations of decreased MPC SkmKO muscle glucose flux into citrate, our data also suggest that pyruvate-alanine cycling is kinetically limited compared to direct mitochondrial pyruvate uptake.
evidence: This is inferred from the decreased citrate enrichment and the additive inhibition data.

claim: During in vivo (U)13C-glucose tracing, the citrate M + 1 and M + 3 isotopologues were decreased in MPC SkmKO muscle, indicating more greatly decreased pyruvate anaplerosis through pyruvate carboxylase compared to forward TCA cycle flux through PDH.
source: During in vivo (U)13C-glucose tracing, the citrate M + 1 and M + 3 isotopologues were decreased in MPC SkmKO muscle, indicating more greatly decreased pyruvate anaplerosis through pyruvate carboxylase compared to forward TCA cycle flux through PDH (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Isotopologue data shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Pyruvate-alanine cycling may be more specifically limiting for pyruvate flux through pyruvate carboxylase and require concomitantly increased glutamine anaplerosis for maintaining TCA cycle flux.
source: Thus, pyruvate-alanine cycling may be more specifically limiting for pyruvate flux through pyruvate carboxylase and require concomitantly increased glutamine anaplerosis for maintaining TCA cycle flux.
evidence: This is inferred from the isotopologue data and glutamine depletion data.

claim: Increased acyl-carnitine utilization, pyruvate-alanine cycling, and anaplerotic glutaminolysis sustain TCA cycle activity when direct pyruvate transport is lost by MPC disruption.
source: Together with observed fatty acid oxidation increases, these data support a model where increased acyl-carnitine utilization, pyruvate-alanine cycling, and anaplerotic glutaminolysis sustain TCA cycle activity when direct pyruvate transport is lost by MPC disruption.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the combined metabolic data.

claim: Body weight, fat mass, and lean mass were not different between WT and MPC SkmKO mice during the first 16 weeks on high fat diet (HFD).
source: Body weight, fat mass, and lean mass were measured twice weekly through the first 16 weeks on HFD and periodically up until age 49 weeks and were not different between genotypes (Figure 6B, C and D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Body composition data during HFD shown in Figure 6B, C, D.

claim: MPC SkmKO mice lost more body fat but equally retained lean mass during weight loss after switching from HFD to normal fat diet (NFD).
source: MPC SkmKO mice lost more body fat but equally retained lean mass during weight loss (Figures 6E, F and G).
evidence: Body composition data during NFD shown in Figure 6E, F, G.

claim: Food intake was not different between WT and MPC SkmKO mice when measured during HFD and 2 weeks into NFD.
source: Food intake was not different between WT and MPC SkmKO mice when measured during HFD and 2 weeks into NFD, when weight loss rate was greatest (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Food intake data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: At both time points (end of HFD and after NFD), MPC SkmKO mice had similar blood glucose but lower serum insulin levels after refeeding.
source: At both time points MPC SkmKO mice had similar blood glucose but lower serum insulin levels after refeeding. (Figure 6H and I).
evidence: Glucose and insulin data shown in Figure 6H and I.

claim: Serum triglyceride levels were lower in MPC SkmKO mice after fasting at the end of the HFD treatment and after both fasting and refeeding after NFD treatment.
source: Serum triglyceride levels were lower in MPC SkmKO mice after fasting at the end of the HFD treatment and after both fasting and refeeding after NFD treatment (Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Triglyceride data referenced in source data.

claim: Constitutive muscle MPC disruption does not prevent HFD-induced obesity but protects against post-prandial hyperinsulinemia during chronic high fat feeding and leads to more rapid onset of leanness when obese mice are returned to NFD.
source: These results demonstrate that constitutive muscle MPC disruption does not prevent HFD-induced obesity but protects against post-prandial hyperinsulinemia during chronic high fat feeding and leads to more rapid onset of leanness when obese mice are returned to NFD.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the HFD/NFD experiment data.

claim: Tamoxifen-inducible MPC skeletal muscle specific knockout mice (iSkmKO) were generated by crossing Mpc1fl/fl mice with mice expressing Cre fused to two modified estrogen receptor elements (mER-Cre-mER), driven by the human skeletal actin promoter (HSA).
source: We generated tamoxifen-inducible MPC skeletal muscle specific knockout mice (iSkmKO) by crossing Mpc1fl/fl mice with mice expressing Cre fused to two modified estrogen receptor elements (mER-Cre-mER), driven by the human skeletal actin promoter (HSA) (McCarthy et al., 2012).
evidence: The generation method is described with citation.

claim: Western blots of skeletal muscles at the end of the study confirmed MPC deletion in iSkmKO mice.
source: Western blots of skeletal muscles at the end of the study confirmed MPC deletion (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Compared to WT mice, MPC iSkmKO mice lost more body weight, which was almost exclusively from fat mass.
source: Compared to WT mice, MPC iSkmKO mice lost more body weight, which was almost exclusively from fat mass (Figure 6K and L).
evidence: Body composition data shown in Figure 6K and L.

claim: MPC iSkmKO mice retained lean mass equal to WT mice.
source: As with constitutive MPC SkmKO mice, iSkmKO mice retained lean mass equal to WT mice (Figure 6M).
evidence: Lean mass data shown in Figure 6M.

claim: No food intake differences were observed between WT and MPC SkmKO mice during normal chow diet feeding after acute deletion.
source: No food intake differences were observed between WT and MPC SkmKO mice during normal chow diet feeding after acute deletion (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Food intake data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Enhanced recovery from obesity after diet switch does not require developmental preconditioning and may be elicited by acute MPC disruption.
source: These results parallel and validate those from constitutive MPC SkmKO mice and demonstrate that enhanced recovery from obesity after diet switch does not require developmental preconditioning and may be elicited by acute MPC disruption.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of constitutive and inducible knockout results.

claim: During type 2 diabetes (T2D) decreased skeletal muscle glucose uptake significantly drives chronic hyperglycemia that leads to microvascular complications and tissue degeneration.
source: During type 2 diabetes (T2D) decreased skeletal muscle glucose uptake significantly drives chronic hyperglycemia that leads to microvascular complications and tissue degeneration (DeFronzo and Tripathy, 2009).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about T2D pathophysiology.

claim: Impaired insulin signaling and consequently blunted GLUT4 transporter translocation to the plasma membrane contribute prominently to decreased muscle glucose uptake in T2D.
source: It is clear that impaired insulin signaling and consequently blunted GLUT4 transporter translocation to the plasma membrane contribute prominently (Kampmann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about mechanisms of insulin resistance.

claim: The glucose-fatty acid or Randle cycle demonstrates that acutely increasing fatty acid supply decreases muscle glucose uptake and oxidation.
source: Over shorter time-scales, this is exemplified by the glucose-fatty acid or Randle cycle, where acutely increasing fatty acid supply decreases muscle glucose uptake and oxidation (Randle et al., 1963).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about the Randle cycle.

claim: During obesity and T2D chronically elevated muscle lipid content and insulin resistance strongly associate, with increased ceramides, diacylglycerols, and mitochondrial acyl-carnitines and -CoAs implicated as causing insulin resistance.
source: Similarly, during obesity and T2D chronically elevated muscle lipid content and insulin resistance strongly associate, with increased ceramides, diacylglycerols, and mitochondrial acyl-carnitines and -CoAs implicated as causing insulin resistance (Koves et al., 2008; Samuel and Shulman, 2016).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about lipid-induced insulin resistance.

claim: A correlate of both acute and chronic lipid oversupply is decreased pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) activity.
source: Notably, a correlate of both conditions is decreased pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) activity (Albers et al., 2015; Pilegaard et al., 2006; Wu et al., 1999).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about PDH activity in metabolic disease.

claim: PDH converts glucose-derived pyruvate into acetyl-CoA inside mitochondria and is therefore essential for complete glucose oxidation.
source: PDH converts glucose-derived pyruvate into acetyl-CoA inside mitochondria and is therefore essential for complete glucose oxidation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PDH function.

claim: In T2D, decreased PDH activity has been hypothesized to impair muscle glucose uptake by metabolic feedback.
source: In T2D, decreased PDH activity has been hypothesized to impair muscle glucose uptake by metabolic feedback (Jeoung, 2015; Nogiec et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a cited hypothesis about PDH and glucose uptake.

claim: Tests of the converse relationship, whether increasing PDH activity increases glucose uptake do not support the idea that glucose oxidation and uptake are obligately connected.
source: Tests of the converse relationship, whether increasing PDH activity increases glucose uptake do not support this idea and demonstrate that glucose oxidation and uptake are not obligately connected.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from cited studies.

claim: Acute chemical PDH activation in rats by dichloroacetate infusion increased muscle glucose oxidation but not uptake.
source: Acute chemical PDH activation in rats by dichloroacetate infusion increased muscle glucose oxidation but not uptake (Small et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited data from a previous study.

claim: Constitutive genetic PDH activation increased muscle glucose oxidation as expected, but led to lipid accumulation, marked insulin resistance, and impaired glucose uptake.
source: Furthermore, constitutive genetic PDH activation increased muscle glucose oxidation as expected, but led to lipid accumulation, marked insulin resistance, and impaired glucose uptake (Rahimi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited data from a previous study.

claim: Neither chronically nor acutely increasing muscle glucose oxidation increased muscle glucose uptake.
source: Thus, neither chronically nor acutely increasing muscle glucose oxidation increased muscle glucose uptake.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the cited PDH activation studies.

claim: The MPC occupies a central metabolic intersection by transporting cytosolic pyruvate into the mitochondrial matrix, thereby linking glycolysis with oxidative phosphorylation.
source: The MPC occupies a central metabolic intersection by transporting cytosolic pyruvate into the mitochondrial matrix, thereby linking glycolysis with oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MPC function.

claim: The genes encoding the MPC were recently discovered.
source: The genes encoding the MPC were recently discovered, and little is known about how mitochondrial pyruvate uptake affects skeletal muscle function (Bricker et al., 2012; Herzig et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about the MPC discovery.

claim: Little is known about how mitochondrial pyruvate uptake affects skeletal muscle function.
source: The genes encoding the MPC were recently discovered, and little is known about how mitochondrial pyruvate uptake affects skeletal muscle function (Bricker et al., 2012; Herzig et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: MPC disruption evoked complex, interconnected changes in muscle and systemic metabolism leading to increased whole-body insulin sensitivity, increased muscle glucose uptake, and attenuation of obesity and T2D.
source: Surprisingly, MPC disruption did not impair muscle glucose uptake. Instead, it evoked complex, interconnected changes in muscle and systemic metabolism leading to increased whole-body insulin sensitivity, increased muscle glucose uptake, and attenuation of obesity and T2D.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: After uptake by skeletal muscle, glucose may be channeled to three major fates: complete mitochondrial oxidation via pyruvate, storage as glycogen, or excretion as lactate.
source: After uptake by skeletal muscle, glucose may be channeled to three major fates: complete mitochondrial oxidation via pyruvate, storage as glycogen, or excretion as lactate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about muscle glucose metabolism.

claim: Muscle glucose uptake and glycolysis are not intrinsically connected to pyruvate oxidation.
source: Importantly, this suggests that muscle glucose uptake and glycolysis are not intrinsically connected to pyruvate oxidation and that lactate excretion functions as flexible offset for balancing glucose uptake with disposal.
evidence: This is inferred from the clamp data showing increased glucose uptake despite decreased pyruvate oxidation.

claim: Lactate excretion functions as flexible offset for balancing glucose uptake with disposal.
source: Importantly, this suggests that muscle glucose uptake and glycolysis are not intrinsically connected to pyruvate oxidation and that lactate excretion functions as flexible offset for balancing glucose uptake with disposal.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing increased lactate excretion in MPC SkmKO mice.

claim: Lactate functions as a systemic energy currency.
source: This is notable given the role of lactate as a systemic energy currency (Brooks, 2018), including recent findings showing that most tissues other than brain, heart, and muscle utilize circulating lactate instead of glucose as their major source of pyruvate for mitochondrial oxidation (Hui et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about lactate metabolism.

claim: Most tissues other than brain, heart, and muscle utilize circulating lactate instead of glucose as their major source of pyruvate for mitochondrial oxidation.
source: This is notable given the role of lactate as a systemic energy currency (Brooks, 2018), including recent findings showing that most tissues other than brain, heart, and muscle utilize circulating lactate instead of glucose as their major source of pyruvate for mitochondrial oxidation (Hui et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from a recent study.

claim: The muscle MPC plays a nodal role in total-body energy supply by controlling circulating lactate fluxes.
source: Thus, our findings demonstrate a nodal role for the muscle MPC in total-body energy supply by controlling circulating lactate fluxes.
evidence: This is inferred from the study findings on lactate and Cori cycling.

claim: The MPC SkmKO mouse leanness is consistent with the unconventional view that elevated Cori Cycling in T2D is adaptive rather than maladaptive.
source: Notably, the MPC SkmKO mouse leanness we observe is consistent with the unconventional view that elevated Cori Cycling in T2D is adaptive rather than maladaptive.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of T2D.

claim: Cori Cycle activity is increased in T2D and characterized as driving hyperglycemia.
source: Cori Cycle activity is increased in T2D and characterized as driving hyperglycemia (Vaag et al., 1995; Zawadzki et al., 1988).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about Cori cycling in T2D.

claim: The full Cori Cycle does not produce net glucose.
source: While this is accurate when considering the gluconeogenic component in isolation, we note that the full Cori Cycle does not produce net glucose.
evidence: This is based on metabolic pathway knowledge.

claim: Muscle glycolysis is increased in T2D, which requires matching glucose uptake.
source: Muscle glycolysis is increased in T2D, which requires matching glucose uptake (Giebelstein et al., 2012; Simoneau and Kelley, 1997; Vaag et al., 1995).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about muscle metabolism in T2D.

claim: The Cori Cycle is futile because the two ATP molecules produced by glycolysis are traded for the six ATP equivalents required for re-synthesis of glucose from pyruvate.
source: The Cori Cycle is futile because the two ATP molecules produced by glycolysis are traded for the six ATP equivalents required for re-synthesis of glucose from pyruvate (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on metabolic pathway knowledge and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The energy-wasting nature of the Cori Cycle is addressed as a problem during cachexia and hyperthyroid states.
source: Surprisingly, while the energy-wasting nature of the Cori Cycle is addressed as a problem during cachexia and hyperthyroid states, it is virtually unaddressed in the diabetes and obesity literature (Huang and Lardy, 1981; Potenza et al., 2009; Tisdale, 2009).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about Cori cycling in different disease contexts.

claim: Elevated Cori Cycling helps solve the T2D metabolic conundrum of how to scavenge circulating glucose while clearing ectopic lipid deposits by oxidation.
source: All other things being equal, elevated Cori Cycling helps solve the T2D metabolic conundrum of how to scavenge circulating glucose while clearing ectopic lipid deposits by oxidation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the potential adaptive role of Cori cycling.

claim: Small metabolic rate increases caused by elevated Cori Cycling can impact long-term body composition.
source: Because obesity often arises from a minimal daily energy surplus accumulated over time, we argue that small metabolic rate increases caused by elevated Cori Cycling can nonetheless impact long-term body composition.
evidence: This is an argument based on the energetics of obesity development.

claim: The physiological changes occurring with skeletal muscle MPC disruption are clearly complex.
source: The physiological changes occurring with skeletal muscle MPC disruption are clearly complex.
evidence: This is stated as an acknowledgment of the complexity of the findings.

claim: By definition, because of the muscle-liver ATP exchange energetics, Cori Cycling increases whole-body energy expenditure.
source: By definition, because of the muscle-liver ATP exchange energetics, Cori Cycling increases whole-body energy expenditure.
evidence: This is based on the energetics of the Cori cycle.

claim: Additional factors that could contribute to MPC SkmKO mouse leanness include altered hypothalamic regulation by unidentified muscle-released serum factors, changes in intramuscular calcium cycling, and yet to be discovered lipolytic cross-talk between muscle and adipose tissue.
source: Additional factors are likely at play as well. These could include altered hypothalamic regulation by unidentified muscle-released serum factors, changes in intramuscular calcium cycling, which is ATP-intensive and known to be intricately connected with metabolism, and yet to be discovered lipolytic cross-talk between muscle and adipose tissue.
evidence: These are speculative mechanisms that could contribute to the phenotype.

claim: PPARγ-sparing thiazolidinedione-like molecules that inhibit the MPC attenuate diabetes in rodents and are now being tested in humans.
source: Though the feasibility of therapeutically targeting the MPC in vivo in humans has yet to be fully tested, we note that PPARγ-sparing thiazolidinedione-like molecules that inhibit the MPC attenuate diabetes in rodents and are now being tested in humans (Colca et al., 2018; McCommis et al., 2015; McCommis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about MPC inhibitors as potential therapeutics.

claim: Pyruvate-alanine cycling can bypass the MPC to partially sustain glucose oxidation.
source: Because pyruvate-alanine cycling can bypass the MPC to partially sustain glucose oxidation, in vivo targeting may therapeutically modulate rather than pathologically constrain mitochondrial metabolism.
evidence: This is based on the study findings on pyruvate-alanine cycling.

claim: In vivo MPC targeting may therapeutically modulate rather than pathologically constrain mitochondrial metabolism.
source: Because pyruvate-alanine cycling can bypass the MPC to partially sustain glucose oxidation, in vivo targeting may therapeutically modulate rather than pathologically constrain mitochondrial metabolism.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about therapeutic potential.

claim: Inactivating human patient MPC1 mutations impair neurological development leading to lasting health problems and in the case of one patient early death.
source: Nonetheless, inactivating human patient MPC1 mutations impair neurological development leading to lasting health problems and in the case of one patient early death (Bricker et al., 2012; Brivet et al., 2003; Oonthonpan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about human MPC1 mutations.

claim: How in vivo pharmacologic MPC modulation affects the function of tissues less metabolically plastic than liver and skeletal muscle, like brain, heart, and kidney, is a critical consideration that will need to be fully addressed.
source: How in vivo pharmacologic MPC modulation affects the function of tissues less metabolically plastic than liver and skeletal muscle, like brain, heart, and kidney, is a critical consideration that will need to be fully addressed.
evidence: This is stated as an important future consideration for therapeutic development.

claim: Important future work includes deciphering the mechanisms by which skeletal muscle MPC disruption increases glucose uptake.
source: Important future work also includes deciphering the mechanisms by which skeletal muscle MPC disruption increases glucose uptake. This will require carefully interrogating insulin and AMPK signaling, glucose transporter regulation, and glycogen metabolism.
evidence: This is stated as a direction for future research.

claim: The findings raise the possibility that selectively decreasing skeletal muscle pyruvate uptake in obese and T2D patients may aid fat mass loss and restoration of whole-body insulin sensitivity.
source: In conclusion, our findings here raise the possibility that selectively decreasing skeletal muscle pyruvate uptake in obese and T2D patients may aid fat mass loss and restoration of whole-body insulin sensitivity.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about potential therapeutic applications.
